defaults.permitted_development: Demolition in England is controlled by the GPDO and heritage legislation, not treated as a free general right. The route depends on what is being removed, whether Part 11 prior approval applies, and whether the site is listed, in a conservation area or otherwise protected. In rural settings, access, waste movements and the treatment of exposed edges after demolition can be the main concerns.

rules.height_rules: There is no demolition height allowance. The real question is the size, type and status of the structure and whether its removal falls within a prior approval route or needs a fuller application.
rules.depth_rules: There is no separate depth rule. Partial demolition, demolition linked to rebuilding, or removal of only part of a structure must be assessed against the actual scope of works and any related development.
rules.boundary_rules: Party walls, adjoining land, hoardings, highway occupation, neighbour safety and the stability of nearby structures are often the most important boundary and site-management issues in a demolition proposal. In rural settings, access, waste movements and the treatment of exposed edges after demolition can be the main concerns.
rules.roof_rules: Removing a roof is not automatically a standalone permitted step. Once roof removal forms part of wider demolition, heritage, structural and weatherproofing issues can change the planning route.
rules.materials_rules: Salvage, asbestos handling, waste removal and making good exposed surfaces are key practical issues. Separate environmental, safety and building-control duties still apply even where the planning route is clear. In rural settings, access, waste movements and the treatment of exposed edges after demolition can be the main concerns.

rules.permitted_development: In Somerset, the route still depends on Part 11, heritage and the actual structure, but access, site safety and the condition of the cleared land often matter as much as the demolition itself.

rules.height_rules: In Somerset, height matters mainly through structural method, visibility and whether tall remnants or plant stand out in open views while the works are underway.
rules.depth_rules: There is no separate depth rule. Partial demolition, demolition tied to rebuilding, or removal of only part of a structure must be judged on the actual scope of works and any linked development.
rules.boundary_rules: In Somerset, site edges often turn on access tracks, protected trees, neighbouring land stability and how rubble, plant and temporary fencing are managed during the works.
rules.roof_rules: Taking off a roof is not automatically a standalone permitted step. Where roof removal forms part of wider demolition, heritage, structural and weatherproofing issues can change the planning route.
rules.materials_rules: Salvage, recycling, asbestos handling, waste removal and making good exposed surfaces are key practical issues. Separate environmental and building-control duties still apply even where the planning route is clear. In rural settings, access, waste movements and the treatment of exposed edges after demolition can be the main concerns.

restrictions.conservation_area: Conservation areas are defined under the legislation as "areas of special architectural or historic interest"
restrictions.listed_building: A listed building is a building included on the 'List of Buildings of Special Architectural or Historic Interest' created by Historic England.
restrictions.article4_notes: An article 4 direction is a direction which enables the local planning authority to withdraw specified permitted development rights across a defined area.

rules.permitted_development: In Bath and North East Somerset, demolition is usually less about a free PD right and more about whether Part 11 applies, what remains attached to neighbours and how the site will be made safe beside the street.

rules.height_rules: In Bath and North East Somerset, there is no demolition height allowance; tall elements, retained facades, scaffold towers and partial structural removal are judged by risk, method and neighbouring conditions rather than by a numeric limit.
rules.depth_rules: There is no separate depth rule. Partial demolition, demolition tied to rebuilding, or removal of only part of a structure must be judged on the actual scope of works and any linked development.
rules.boundary_rules: In Bath and North East Somerset, the real boundary issue is usually attachment: party walls, neighbouring structure stability, scaffold oversail, highway occupation and keeping adjoining homes safe and weather-tight.
rules.roof_rules: Taking off a roof is not automatically a standalone permitted step. Where roof removal forms part of wider demolition, heritage, structural and weatherproofing issues can change the planning route.
rules.materials_rules: Salvage, recycling, asbestos handling, waste removal and making good exposed surfaces are key practical issues. Separate environmental and building-control duties still apply even where the planning route is clear. In rural settings, access, waste movements and the treatment of exposed edges after demolition can be the main concerns.

restrictions.conservation_area: Demolition in a conservation area can need planning permission for relevant demolition and a much closer heritage review, even where the structure looks minor.
restrictions.listed_building: Demolition of a listed building, or of a curtilage structure protected as part of it, needs listed building consent.
restrictions.article4_notes: Article 4 directions can remove fallback demolition rights in selected locations, so check the site's designation before assuming a prior approval or permitted route still applies.
